finding.claim: DELETE /projects/:id lets any authenticated user delete any other user's project. The ownership predicate authorized() is called but its boolean return is discarded, so no check gates the delete.
finding.source: HTTP DELETE /projects/:id; :id from req.params (api.js:17). Precondition: authenticated user with req.user populated by unseen upstream middleware.

trace.note: project = req.store.projects.get(req.params.id) loads any project by ID
authorized(req.user, project) evaluates ownership but return value is discarded

finding.guards_checked: authorize() (api.js:4-10) throws on non-owner but is not called on this route; authorized() (api.js:12-14) is a pure predicate that never throws; no route-level middleware in file; mount point and upstream guard not present in repo, so not verified.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. authorize() (api.js:4-10) would throw on non-owner, but it is not called on the DELETE route (api.js:16-21). authorized() (api.js:12-14) is a pure predicate whose boolean is discarded at api.js:18, so project.delete at api.js:19 runs unconditionally. No route-level middleware in api.js. The mount point and any upstream middleware are not in the repo.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches: api.js:17 loads the project by ID, api.js:18 calls authorized() as a bare statement with its result discarded, and api.js:19 deletes unconditionally before the 204 at api.js:20, so any authenticated user can delete another user's project. The one caveat is that an upstream mount-level middleware not in this repo could enforce ownership on :id, but nothing visible here shows one, so the finding stands on the code available.

finding.claim: Inconsistent admin checks: authorize() uses truthy !user.isAdmin while authorized() uses strict isAdmin === true. If isAdmin can be a truthy non-boolean, PUT /projects/:id/name grants non-owner access. Unconfirmed.
finding.source: req.user.isAdmin, origin not shown in repo
finding.sink: authorize() conditional at api.js:5, used by PUT at api.js:25
finding.guards_checked: Strict boolean check present in authorized() but not used by PUT; how req.user is constructed not visible.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at api.js:5 throws 403 for non-owner non-admin and is called as a bare statement at api.js:25, so it does block the PUT path for ordinary users. No code in the repo shows how req.user.isAdmin is constructed, so whether it can be a truthy non-boolean is unknown.
verdict.reason: The trace lines at api.js:5, api.js:13 and api.js:25 are accurate, but exploitability depends on req.user.isAdmin being a truthy non-boolean, and the code that builds req.user is not in the repo. Separately, api.js:18 discards the boolean from authorized(), so DELETE /projects/:id has no effective authorization, a stronger issue the candidate did not report.

finding.claim: Nonexistent project ID causes TypeError (500) in DELETE and PUT instead of 404, giving an existence oracle. No authorization bypass.
finding.source: req.params.id for an ID that does not exist
finding.sink: resource.ownerId dereference on undefined at api.js:13 / api.js:6 via api.js:18 and api.js:25

trace.note: store.get returns undefined for missing ID
authorize() dereferences undefined resource on PUT

finding.guards_checked: Throw occurs before any mutation, so no state change; hardening only.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only checks are authorized() at api.js:12-14 and authorize() at api.js:4-10. For a missing ID, authorized() dereferences undefined at api.js:13 and authorize() does the same at api.js:5, so no guard prevents the TypeError. The authorized() call at api.js:18 is a bare statement whose boolean result is discarded.
verdict.reason: The existence oracle holds: a missing ID throws a TypeError at api.js:13 (via api.js:18 on DELETE) and api.js:5 (via api.js:25 on PUT), which returns a 500 while existing IDs don't. However, the candidate's "No authorization bypass" claim is wrong: api.js:18 discards the boolean from authorized(), so DELETE /projects/:id at api.js:19 deletes any existing project for any authenticated user regardless of ownership, which is a much more serious authorization flaw that should be reported separately. Caveat: store.get returning undefined (api.js:17) depends on the store implementation, which is not in the directory, but the oracle claim is conditional on that behaviour.

finding.claim: PUT /projects/:id/name stores req.body.name without type or length validation; undefined, objects, or unbounded strings are persisted and returned.
finding.source: req.body.name from the request body, by project owner or admin
finding.sink: project.name assignment at api.js:26, returned via res.json at api.js:27
finding.guards_checked: No validation middleware in file; rendering of name by consumers not in repo. Data-integrity hardening, no privilege gain.

verdict.guard_found: api.js:25 `authorize(req.user, project)` throws a 403 unless the requester is the owner or an admin. It is a bare call whose throw is not caught, so it does block non-owners. It does not validate the type or length of `req.body.name`, which is the claimed flaw.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (api.js:26 assigns req.body.name unvalidated, api.js:27 returns it), but the only callers who can reach it are the project owner or an admin (api.js:5, 25), who can already set this name to any value, so no privilege is gained; the remaining issue is input hardening with no security impact, which the candidate itself concedes.
